How your AI agent can pay with your credit card, without ever holding it:

1. Your card stays stored in a trusted wallet.

2. When your agent goes to buy something, the wallet creates an agentic token: a stand-in card number that only works at that store, with limits like "don't spend more than $100."

3. Your agent hands the token to the store.

4. The store runs it through its usual payment processor, and the charge lands on your real card, with your rewards and card benefits intact.

"AOL was a helpful set of training wheels for getting everyone online, but the open web ultimately won. We think the same thing will happen with agents as well."

Chinese government bonds returned about 9% in dollar terms over the past year, beating US and global bonds, both slightly negative. Two forces drove it: a yuan up roughly 5% on the dollar, and local yields grinding lower as growth and prices deflate.

Falling yields mean rising bond prices, and in China they are falling because the economy is sick. A world-beating return is the deflation trade in a bull costume.

Every month, Indian importers buy more dollars than exporters sell. In the latest month, importer dollar purchases ran near $75 billion, the most this year, against far smaller exporter sales. That is constant, one-way pressure on the currency.

Intervention can smooth the slide. The standing bid for dollars is why the rupee keeps grinding to new lows.

India's short-dated forward premium has spiked toward 5%, near the top of its range, driven by the RBI's dollar-rupee swaps as it leans against the currency's slide. Paying up to hedge dollars is the tell that the defense is getting expensive.

A central bank can slow a falling currency. It cannot repeal the reason it is falling.
